Pocock says his constituents contact him most about ‘human rights and the Gaza genocide’. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Australian politics Crossbench MPs launch push to stop Australian military exports being used in human rights breaches ‘Red lines’ legislation would forbid defence equipment technology or services being used, includes parts for F-35 fighter jets Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Krishani Dhanji Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Crossbench MPs including David Pocock and Sophie Scamps will put pressure on the Albanese government to ban Australian goods from being used by the Israeli military – including for F-35 fighter jets – by introducing a bill designed to force it to adhere to international obligations. The group’s “red lines” legislation, to be presented on Monday, would outlaw defence equipment, technology or services being used where they could breach Australia’s international human rights obligations. They hope the bill would end Australia’s involvement in manufacturing parts of the F-35 aircraft used by the Israeli air force in Gaza to “strike terror targets and assist ground forces in very close proximity strikes” – which the government has been under increasing pressure to stop. “Of all the issues many people contact me about, human rights and the Gaza genocide is by far the biggest,” Pocock said. “I have received thousands of emails from Canberrans desperately concerned by the indiscriminate killing we have seen overseas.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The foreign minister, Penny Wong, has previously described Australia’s contributions to the F-35 supply chain as “ non-lethal in nature ”. The defence minister, Richard Marles, has accused critics of “misinformation” and said Australia has contributed to program for decades as part of a multi-lateral agreement with Lockheed Martin in the US, rather than with Israel directly. The prime minister was roundly criticised last week, including from within his own ranks , for not following the UK and other like-minded countries in banning trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The crossbench group – which also includes the Greens and independents Lidia Thorpe, Andrew Wilkie and Fatima Payman – say their bill could also prevent companies and institutions investing in activities connected to illegal settlements and serious international law violations. The proponents of the laws say they would put Australia’s legislation in line with its international human rights obligations, and establish an independent anti-genocide commissioner. Large companies, defence businesses and commonwealth entities would also be forced to report and intervene on genocide risks in their operations and supply chains. The Greens’ deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi, challenged the government to “prove that all their talk about international law and human rights actually means something”. “This package is far from radical and delivers exactly what Australians expect of their government. Australian governments and corporations should not be sending military parts, trading with, or profiting from, a genocide,” she said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The bills are backed by international law advocates and experts including the former president of the Australian Human Rights Commission, Gillian Triggs, and the executive director of the Australian Centre for International Justice, Rawan Arraf. Scamps said the legislation would help ensure business and the government were not “unknowingly complicit in war crimes and genocide and other human rights violations”. “This is not about a single country, there are grievous human rights abuses going on all around the world,” she said. “It is not nearly good enough for our government to say they are not sure if components we manufacture here in Australia are being used in F-35s that have killed tens of thousands of people in Gaza.” Thorpe said bill – to be concurrently introduced in the house and Senate this week – was about upholding fundamental human rights that the government “is already committed to under international law”. Labor is not expected to support the private member’s bill. https://www.politico.eu/article/calin-ge.text: Former presidential candidate Călin Georgescu was detained Monday on suspicion of fraud by Romanian police and the Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT). The ultranationalist politician shot to prominence when he unexpectedly won the first round of the November 2024 presidential election, snapping up 23% of the vote . But the Constitutional Court annulled the election in December that year and barred Georgescu from running again due to his campaign’s links to a Russian influence operation. Romanian authorities are investigating Georgescu for committing fraud and forming an organized criminal group that prosecutors say defrauded a Romanian businessman by promising access to multimillion-euro foreign bank financing in exchange for cash guarantees. Advertisement Advertisement “The perpetrators acted by misleading and deceiving a Romanian businessmen … the members of the organized crime group aimed to obtain the financial guarantees deposited by the victim to access the respective credits,” a DIICOT press release noted. The group allegedly failed to deliver on its promises, and the victim lost “more than €1.1 million.” The former presidential candidate is already facing two other criminal cases: one over allegedly acting against Romania’s constitutional order by planning a violent coup , and another over allegedly promoting fascist ideology. Commenting on the earlier investigations, Georgescu protested his innocence and said the cases were “politically motivated.” Several dozen supporters of Georgescu gathered Monday in front of the DIICOT headquarters, where he will be brought in for questioning, Romanian media reported. Photograph: CLPRESS/ABACA/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Students take part in a blockade outside Voltaire high school in Paris's 11th arrondissement. Photograph: CLPRESS/ABACA/Shutterstock France France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country Jon Henley in Paris Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.52 EDT Last modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 15.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country. Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday. About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille. View image in fullscreen The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves. Photograph: CLPress/Abaca/Shutterstock Nearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 300 police and dozens of firefighters, teachers and pupils have been injured. The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests. Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles, with the interior ministry announcing an internal police investigation after accusations of excessive force and brutality by officers against three pupils. Rubbish bins have been set on fire outside many schools and more serious arson attempts have been reported inside some buildings. Fire damage in one school in Nantes in the north-west was so extensive that it will stay closed for a month, authorities said. View image in fullscreen Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests. Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty Images In the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting bins on fire would protest “with words”. Students were protesting “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”, she told AFP. In Strasbourg in the north-east, tram services were temporarily suspended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said, after protesting students obstructed the tracks with crowd control barriers. “There are 35 of us per classroom,” one 17-year-old Strasbourg student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.” Several bin fires were also reported in the southern city of Toulouse; while in Lille, young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop. In Marseille, there were attempts to light fires inside two schools. In one, a teacher was splashed with petrol. View image in fullscreen Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles. Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty Images While many teachers and several headteachers have reported being physically threatened and sometimes attacked, some support their pupils. Juliette Estiville, a high-school Spanish teacher in Paris, said that the police response had disgusted her. “I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.” The government has accused the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the protests, with several LFI MPs and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, cheered at demonstrations. The party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, insisted on Thursday that LFI backed “non-violent methods of struggle” and added that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”. In Vilnius, an interactive video screen offers a window into cities around the world, showing them in real time. One city may still be enjoying the afternoon while another is already approaching evening. At the end of October, Lithuania and the rest of the European Union will once again turn their clocks back one hour, shifting to standard, or winter, time. For some Lithuanians, the twice-yearly ritual has long been an annoyance. âI donât like turning the clocks,â one woman told LRT TV. âItâs like we gain an hour in the autumn, but then, once we get used to it, they change something again. Iâd really like them to finally make a decision.â Another passerby said the time should simply remain fixed. âThereâs no need to turn them back and forth. We need one consistent time â either winter or summer,â he said. âIt affects you. Your mood is completely different in the morning and evening.â Transport Minister Juras Taminskas agrees. He has been trying since the beginning of the year to persuade the Baltic and Nordic countries to agree on ending the practice. Juras Taminskas | E. BlaÅ¾ys / LRT Even his dog, he jokes, does not understand the clock change. âThey used to say cows donât understand the clock change. Well, my dog doesnât understand it either, because when you change the time, you have to take him out for a walk at a different time,â Taminskas said. âIâm in favour of not changing the clocks.â Taminskas hopes to make the issue part of Lithuaniaâs agenda when it takes over the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union for six months starting in January. He acknowledges that reaching an agreement could be difficult, particularly with southern European countries. âConsidering the current political situation, when there are so many important issues and challenges, not being able to agree on something as basic as this â an issue that has been dividing people emotionally, psychologically and physically for decades â is, to put it mildly, embarrassing,â he said. But Å½ygimantas Mauricas, chief economist at Luminor bank, is less optimistic. Changing time | J. StaceviÄius / LRT âLooking at how difficult it is to reach agreement on other issues in the EU, success is probably unlikely,â he said. The biggest obstacle, Mauricas said, is not necessarily whether Europe should stop changing its clocks, but which time it should keep. For Lithuania, that choice presents a particular dilemma. Summer time would provide more daylight during the evening and, Mauricas said, could be more favourable for peopleâs health because it would maximise the number of daylight hours when people are awake and active. But there are also economic considerations. Lithuania, like the other Baltic countries and Finland, are in the Eastern European Time zone (UTC+2), while most of the rest of the EU is one hour behind. Having the same time as major trading partners can make cross-border business easier. Germany is particularly important for Lithuania, Mauricas said. But there is hard geography which can be stretched only so much. As it is, Spain and Poland are separated by nearly 3,000 kilometres but operate on the same clock. Å½ygimantas Mauricas | D. Umbrasas / LRT âEssentially, thatâs completely absurd,â Mauricas said. The arrangement means Spain sacrifices some morning daylight while Poland gives up some daylight in the evening. If Lithuania adopted permanent winter time to align with Poland, it would similarly lose brighter evenings. âBecause we are next to Poland, we would also sacrifice our bright evenings if we joined them,â Mauricas said. âBut economically, it would probably be more beneficial.â That could create another source of public frustration, he said. âIf permanent winter time were introduced, believe me, there would be even more complaints,â Mauricas said. A clock (associative image) | AP His calculations suggest Lithuania would lose about 40 minutes of daylight if it permanently adopted winter time. Transport Minister Taminskas says the decision should ultimately be made jointly by the EU member states. He says representatives should vote on which time to retain and accept the outcome of the majority. Lithuania already has an initial agreement with the Baltic and Nordic countries in favour of permanent summer time, he said. Polandâs position will also be important because neighbouring countries benefit from having a common position. Previous public opinion surveys in Lithuania have consistently shown support for keeping summer time year-round. The Transport Ministry does not plan to conduct a new survey, however, saying such polls can leave countries stuck in the same arguments. For now, there is no agreement. So on the night of October 24-25, Lithuanians will once again turn their clocks back an hour â gaining an extra hour of sleep, but also seeing autumn evenings suddenly getting much darker.
